subtype: Approach: checking legal terms with a lawyer [Action]
passage:
I'm Santosh, and looking back, the most useful money I spent that year was on a lawyer. The paper from the investor was twenty pages, and I had read it three times without really understanding a line about "drag-along".
So I booked an hour and a half with Siddharth, who works with startups. At the start Siddharth said, "I can explain how clauses like these generally work. What you agree to is your decision, and it's worth having someone qualified read your exact papers too."
We went clause by clause in ordinary language. When I got to the drag-along one, my shoulders came down. I understood what it meant for me if a buyer arrived.
I went home with a list of four questions, not a guess.

qa.q: How long did Santosh book with Siddharth?
qa.a: Santosh booked an hour and a half.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after understanding the drag-along clause?
qa.a: Santosh felt relieved and less afraid, shown by the shoulders coming down.

qa.q: What could Santosh do next with the list of four questions?
qa.a: Santosh could take the questions back to Siddharth or to the investor and ask for the answers in writing before signing.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the role in this meeting?
qa.a: Siddharth sees it as explaining how such clauses generally work and leaving the decision to Santosh, since that is what was said at the start.

grounding: The account shows a founder paying a startup lawyer to explain shareholder agreement clauses in ordinary language before signing.

passage:
Mentor's note, 12 September.
I went with Jatin today to the startup lawyer he had hired to go through the shareholder agreement before signing. He had printed all forty pages and marked every clause he didn't understand in yellow. There was a lot of yellow.
The lawyer took two hours and explained each marked clause in plain language: what the investors' approval rights would mean in practice, what would happen to his shares if he left early, how a future sale would be split. She was careful to say this was a general explanation of how such terms usually work, and that Jatin should ask again if anything changed.
Jatin asked good questions, including two he admitted felt "stupid". On the way out he said he had been close to signing last week on trust. We agreed he would send the lawyer's notes to his co-founder before any decision.
— Vaibhav

qa.q: How many pages was the agreement?
How did Jatin feel asking the two questions he called stupid?
qa.a: He felt a bit embarrassed but asked anyway, showing he cared more about understanding than looking clever.

qa.q: What else could Jatin do before signing?
qa.a: Share the lawyer's notes with his co-founder and list any terms he still wants to discuss with the investors.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Jatin's approach?
qa.a: Vaibhav sees careful preparation, the yellow marks and good questions, compared with nearly signing on trust.

grounding: It shows a founder paying a startup lawyer to explain the shareholder agreement in plain terms before signing, as general understanding rather than guesswork.

passage:
Rajni's diary, Thursday.
Spent ₹25,000 today on two hours with a startup lawyer, and Karthik grumbled about the fee all the way there. By the way back, the grumbling had stopped.
We'd been about to sign the shareholder agreement after skimming it at midnight. Today the lawyer went through it clause by clause. One line I had read as "standard" actually meant the investors could block our next round unless they approved it. Another explained what happens to our shares if one of us leaves in the first two years, which neither of us had understood at all.
The lawyer kept saying, "This is how these terms generally work; the choices are yours." No telling us what to do, just making it clear.
Now we have a list of three things to ask the investors about. I feel much less like we're signing in the dark.

qa.q: How much did the two hours with the lawyer cost?
How does Rajni feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Rajni feels much less like they are signing in the dark: relieved and clearer.

qa.q: What should Rajni and Karthik do with the three questions?
qa.a: Raise them with the investors before signing, and go back to the lawyer if the answers change the terms.

qa.q: How did Karthik's view of the fee change?
qa.a: Karthik grumbled on the way there but stopped on the way back, having seen its value.

grounding: It shows founders paying a lawyer to explain their shareholder agreement clause by clause in plain terms before signing, rather than guessing.
